facts.claim: "Lottery" is a single by American rapper Latto featuring Congolese-Canadian singer Lu Kala. It was released February 17, 2023 on Streamcut/RCA Records.
WhoSampled lists the producers as Dr. Luke and Brandon Benjamin.
Revolt credits the production to Dr. Luke and Rocco Did It Again!. Rate Your Music lists Rocco Did It Again! as a composer and lyricist, not a producer.

Writing credits include Alyssa Stephens (Latto), Lusamba Vanessa Kalala (Lu Kala), Lukasz Gottwald (Dr. Luke), Brandon Benjamin, Lauren Larue, LunchMoney Lewis, Randall Hammers, Rocco Valdes and Steph Jones.

Rate Your Music credits Lauren Larue and Steph Jones with background vocals, Kalani Thompson as additional producer and engineer, Tyler Sheppard as engineer, Clint Gibbs as mixing engineer and Dale Becker as mastering engineer.
Lu Kala said she started writing the hook in March 2022, according to an Entertainment Tonight interview cited by the fan wiki. Latto later added her verses.

Latto said she found exploring pop "fun." She said the bigger, more commercial beats led her to approach the sessions with a broader mind, which meant a lot of second-guessing and re-cutting. WhoSampled attributes this to a Cosmopolitan interview.
The video, directed by Chandler Lass, uses disco and casino sets and shows the pair riding in a limo through Las Vegas. Latto said the visuals flowed with the beat, matching its 70s disco flavor.
Uproxx described the track as a groovy, disco-inspired dancefloor anthem. In it, Latto lays down rules for persistent men, with lottery puns throughout.
The song gave Lu Kala her first entry on the Billboard Hot 100 and the Canadian Hot 100. She and Latto performed it at the 2023 Billboard Women in Music event on March 1.

research.lineage: A disco-inflected pop-rap single from Atlanta-area rapper Latto, reuniting her with producer Dr. Luke after her 2022 album 777, in the vein of the bright dancefloor pop he produced for Doja Cat's "Say So".

draft:
Every line of the hook on **Lottery** starts with a condition. "If I let you put your hands all over me," Lu Kala sings, and the sentence runs through four ifs before it reaches a payoff that hasn't happened yet. That's the power move of the whole song: the prize is described in loving detail and never handed over. The man is holding a ticket. The women are running the draw.

Lu Kala, the Congolese-Canadian singer, started writing that hook in March 2022, and Latto added her verses later. You can hear the split. The hook teases and promises. Latto's verses lay out the terms. She opens with a laugh and a self-crowning, then stacks lottery puns: scratch-offs, jackpots, Mega Millions, a body turned into the winning number. Uproxx heard it as a set of rules for persistent men, and that's the right frame.

What lifts it above a pun parade is that the rules contradict each other, and Latto lets them. In one verse she wants a boss who doesn't care what the bill costs. In the next: "You gotta work for this, can't purchase this." Both are true to her. She likes being spent on and refuses to be bought, and her pride lives in the gap between those positions. It's the voice of someone who knows her worth and won't let a wallet settle the question. The swagger works as a fence as much as a flirt.

Dr. Luke's production reunites him with Latto after her 2022 album 777, in the vein of the bright dancefloor pop he made with Doja Cat on "Say So." Latto has said exploring pop was fun, and that the bigger, more commercial beats had her second-guessing and re-cutting. She described the beat as having a 70s disco flavor, and Chandler Lass's video, with its disco and casino sets and limo ride through Las Vegas, follows it there. Under her verses, though, the drums are trap: kick, snare and hi-hats, a low sustained synth bass holding the roots, a higher synth repeating a short phrase. The groove is relaxed at a moderate tempo, with a slight swing. The mix is dry, clean and upfront, and Latto raps right on top of it, precise and confident, with no harmonies to soften her.

The song gave Lu Kala her first Billboard Hot 100 entry. It closes in the conditional where it began, with Latto adding one more line: "You know you hit the lotto, right?"

That last "right?" is the hook: it puts you in the seat of the person who decides, and it makes withholding sound like the best feeling in the room.
